How I work, in three habits

Whether the brief says product, branding or a wedding website, I end up asking the same question: what is this person feeling right now, and what would make the next ten seconds easier for them?

one

Start from the worry, not the feature list

A grade 12 student doesn’t want “a diagnostic test.” They want to know where they are losing points. I write the screen around that question first.

two

Small details carry the feeling

A guest seeing their own name. A photo that prints when you press a button. A bottle pretty enough to leave out. I keep those details consistent by designing them as a system, not one screen at a time.

three

Build it to find out

I prototype with AI coding tools (Claude Code, Antigravity) on Next.js and GSAP, put a working version in front of real users, watch what they do, and adjust. Most of my best decisions came from that loop.

01NaviEdu · K-12 adaptive learning

From one mock exam to a 15-minute daily habit

Role
Product Owner: research, prototype, handoff
Team
~10 people, startup
For
Grade 12 students preparing for the national graduation exam (THPT), Math
Live
k12.naviedu.vn/thi-thu

The problem

NaviEdu’s mission is personalised learning for K-12 students in Vietnam, at a cost ordinary families can afford. Most exam prep treats every student the same: the same thick books, the same long classes. A student scoring 5 and a student aiming for 9 get the same plan, and both waste time on what they already know.

What I learned from others

I studied the user journeys of products that already do this well, mainly Squirrel AI (China) and IXL. Both diagnose before they teach, break a subject into small knowledge points, and turn mastery into a visible path. I mapped their flows step by step, then rebuilt the idea around a Vietnamese grade 12 student with little time and even less patience.

step 1

Mock exam

A full THPT-format Math paper. Students get an estimated score right away and see themselves on a leaderboard.

90 minutes
step 2

Topic check

Short assessments across 10 exam topics (trigonometry, exponentials & logs, integrals, solid geometry…) to find the exact gaps.

20–30 min total
step 3

Personal sprint

A daily plan to fill those gaps, ordered from the foundations that appear most in the exam to advanced topics, depending on the score band the student wants.

from 15 min a day

diagnose first, then prescribe. the order matters.

I built the first working prototype of this flow myself, tested it with students and parents, then turned what I saw into the flows and requirements the engineering team shipped from.

Mock exam room“Know right away where you lose points.” The headline answers the student’s real question.

Build your own pathTwo assessments, explained in plain words before anything starts.

Unlock in two stepsA 0/2 progress bar turns testing into a small quest instead of a chore.

Honest about effort“About 20–30 minutes” and exactly what you get back, before you commit.

Topic deep-diveEach answer is treated as a measurement of a gap, not just right or wrong.

swipe for more screens →

UX decisions I’d defend
Lead with the answer they want

The page says Thi thử: biết ngay mất điểm ở đâu (know where you lose points), not “take our test.” The benefit comes before the effort.

Say how long it takes

Students quit things that feel endless. Every step shows its time cost, and the daily plan starts at 15 minutes so it fits around school.

Order by payoff

The plan fills high-frequency foundations first. Advanced topics only appear if the student’s target band needs them.

Give it social energy

A public leaderboard turned a lonely practice paper into something students talked about and came back to.

300+
Result

grade 12 students sat the NaviEdu mock exam and entered the diagnostic flow. I also named and designed the brand for the grade 12 product line, Mát Máth, including its mascot.

A diagnosis only helps if the student believes it and comes back tomorrow.What NaviEdu taught me

why I started Glow

Most online wedding invitations in Vietnam are templates: the same layout with the names swapped. But a wedding belongs to two specific people, and in this era the invitation link is the first touchpoint guests have with the day, often days before the ceremony. I wanted to serve couples who care about the small, considered details, and to make the guest’s first tap feel like the couple. Glow is also my playground: every couple is a new design concept and a new interaction to try with real users and a real deadline.

tap to print
Quốc Anh & Diệp Khanh

A save-the-date you print yourself

The couple wanted it to feel handmade and playful, like a knitted sweater and a photo booth. The guest presses Print now, a little printer feeds out the couple’s photo as a postage stamp, and their names land underneath.

  • The first action is a reward: one tap and something physical seems to happen.
  • The album is a film roll you swipe; the schedule photos take a tap to “drop a heart.”
  • Copy is in the couple’s own voice (“tụi mình”), so it reads like a message from friends.

tap to open
Quốc Phong & Huyền My

Opening a door in the Hue citadel

The couple shot their photos at the imperial citadel in Hue and married at Fairmont Hanoi. The invitation opens like a palace screen: tap Mở thiệp (open), a golden sun rises behind an ink orchid, butterflies drift in, and the screen gives way to the couple in áo ngũ thân.

  • Vietnamese and English toggle, for family abroad.
  • The lunar date sits next to the solar one, because grandparents read the lunar calendar.
  • Step-by-step directions to the ballroom inside a big hotel, where guests usually get lost.
Open the live site ↗
personal link
Đức Anh & Diễm My

Every guest gets their own invitation

Each guest receives a personal link. Opening it, a sheer veil sweeps across a sunset sea and the invitation addresses them by name: Dear Ms. Sonia Chen. After they reply, the RSVP section shows their table number, so there is no hunting for a seating chart on the night.

  • Being named makes a mass invitation feel personal.
  • The RSVP screen changes after replying: from a form to “Your table: 4.”
  • An evening timeline that reminds guests to keep their lucky-draw number.
Open the live site ↗
draw to reveal
Ying-Chuan & Minh Anh

A blank page guests sketch open

A cross-border couple with many guests flying in from overseas. The site opens on a blank sheet that says “Let’s sketch with us.” Wherever the guest draws, the illustrated save-the-date appears under their finger, until the couple dancing on a champagne tower is fully revealed.

  • The guest literally makes the invitation appear: a playful, memorable first touch.
  • Sections for e-visa steps, airport fast track, where to stay and what to eat in Vietnam, because foreign guests had these questions before any others.
  • English first, Vietnamese one tap away.

Behind the studio: systems & automation

Glow is a one-person studio running 7–8 freelance designers and several weddings at once. That only works because the repeat work is a system, not a to-do list.

A CRM for the studio

One tracker for every client, project stage and payment, plus a freelancer roster that records each designer’s strengths, so each new brief goes to the right person.

Smart RSVP hub

Couples don’t want to chase guests on Zalo. A central hub I built in Apps Script sends every site’s replies into the couple’s own Google Sheet, adapts to each event’s questions (plus-ones, bride or groom side, dietary needs) and supports per-guest links.

A base template, not a blank page

Every new site starts from a shared set of sections and components (hero, love story, agenda, RSVP…), so time goes into the concept and the motion instead of rebuilding the basics.

Glow Archive

An internal workspace I’m designing where freelancers keep each project’s moodboard and handoff assets side by side, and learn from each other’s work. I cut tagging and profile pages to keep the core flow simple.

Open Glow Archive ↗
AI agents with memory

I wrote skill files and an agent memory system for Claude Code, so AI agents keep the context of each client project instead of starting cold every session.

Email automation

For the Enchanted Cruise event, an n8n workflow handled the RSVP emails, so guests heard back as soon as they replied.

How a project runs: discovery chat and moodboard → one concept that only fits the couple → motion and build in code → testing on the phones their parents actually use → RSVP wiring and launch. Also: Linh & Tony and other couples.

$2K+
Result

in revenue within five months of launching, with every site built and shipped by me.

03THOMEST by PinaGreen · homecare

Making housework feel like taking care of yourself

Role
Head of Marketing: brand & design system
Since
October 2026, pre-launch
Product
Pineapple-enzyme dish soap (Sạch) and hand wash (iu)
For
Urban 22–30 year-olds who live green

The ambition

Vietnam’s cleaning shelf is full of harsh chemical detergents, and most people treat housework as a burden to get through. PinaGreen’s founding team wants to change the experience of cleaning itself, starting with products made from enzymes in pineapple peel. The first two are a dish soap and a hand wash.

Brand as user experience

For a product you touch every day, the brand is the experience: the scent when you pump it, whether the bottle is nice enough to leave by the sink, the words on the label at 11pm with a pile of dishes. I framed the audience, built the idea From Homecare to Selfcare, and wrote the brand system the team designs from: guideline, key messages, design system, social and website rules.

Me, outside the screen

I’m a lifelong learner, and my comfort zone sits somewhere outside my safe zone. Since I turned 20, every year has had one adventure.

2025

A road trip the length of Vietnam. North to south, in a country I thought I already knew.

2026

Three months backpacking Malaysia and Indonesia, including six weeks volunteering as an English teacher in Solo, with students from kindergarten to working adults.

2027

Still unwritten. That’s the part I like.

2025 · road trip2026 · backpacking

I feel most alive when I’m learning about people and culture. In a classroom in Solo, without a shared language, I had to read faces, rebuild a lesson halfway through, and find the gesture that made a shy kid brave enough to answer. Living with host families showed me how much of “welcome” lives in small things: a seat saved for you, a dish someone explains, your name remembered on the second day.

The further I go, the more I believe design is a way of paying attention to people who are not like me. The interfaces I make will be used by a student cramming at midnight, a grandmother opening a link her grandson sent, a stranger in a country they’ve never visited. I want each of them to feel what I felt on the road: that someone thought about them before they arrived.
